channel.title: ResearchBuzz - Transformed
channel.description: News and resources covering social media, search engines, databases, archives, and other such information collections. Since 1998.

item.title: New database maps Canada’s $17.3 billion DAF landscape and where philanthropic wealth is concentrated
item.description: Future of Good: “A new database that maps Canada’s donor-advised funds (DAFs) landscape, shows that a significant share of the country’s charitable assets are concentrated in a small number of organizations. The new database from WellFunded, is intended to make information about organizations that sponsor DAFs and the assets they manage easier to understand, said co-creator and CEO Jeff Golby.”

item.title: New global database advances critical minerals research
item.description: Geoscience Australia: “The Critical Minerals in Ores – Mineral Chemistry database, known as CMiO-MIN, has been developed through the Critical Minerals Mapping Initiative (CMMI), an international partnership between Geoscience Australia, the United States Geological Survey and the Geological Survey of Canada. The release adds approximately 13,000 data points from ore-related mineral samples collected from deposits around the world.”

item.title: DH2026 Video Archive Now Available
item.description: Alliance of Digital Humanities Organizations: “One week has passed since DH2026: Engagement closed in Daejeon, and the recordings many of you have been asking for are now online. A single YouTube playlist collects the conference highlights, the Opening Ceremony, the keynote lectures, and the Closing Ceremony from the 36th annual conference of the Alliance of Digital Humanities Organizations, held 27–31 July 2026 at the Daejeon Convention Center.”

item.title: You may now qualify for Google’s new Search profile, here’s how to check
item.description: Android Authority: “If you have ever wished Google Search could give your favorite creators or publishers something closer to a social media profile, Google is getting there. The company launched Search profiles in June, giving eligible publishers and creators a dedicated space to bring their websites, social accounts, videos, and posts together. Now, Google is making those profiles considerably easier to get.”

item.title: Google co-founder Sergey Brin has now spent $100 million to fight the billionaire tax
item.description: TechCrunch: “Google co-founder Sergey Brin has donated another $20 million to Build a Better California, an organization advocating against California’s proposed billionaire tax, according to a new filing. That means that the world’s fourth-richest man, whose net worth hovers around $267 billion, has now spent more than $100 million to avoid an estimated $13.3 billion tax payment.”

item.title: Reddit stock jumps on inclusion in S&P 500
item.description: CNBC: “Reddit shares rose 11% in extended trading on Thursday on the social media company’s inclusion in the S&P 500. The company will join the index on Aug 18, replacing AvalonBay Communities, according to a release from S&P Dow Jones Indices.”

item.title: I Tried the Android App That’s Helping People Around the World Bypass Censorship Laws
item.description: Lifehacker: “…the Tor project has teamed up with the Bloco Android app studio to release another app focused on privacy and anonymity: Snowflake Volunteer. This isn’t only bout keeping your own browsing safe and secure—if you install it on your Android phone, you’re helping other people circumvent censorship restrictions in their current location, donating part of your connection to the web so that they can get online at all.”

item.title: Phoebe Gates knew Phia shopping app took credit for sales it didn’t drive
item.description: Bloomberg: “Phia co-founders Phoebe Gates and Sophia Kianni pushed for features in the e-commerce startup’s software that took credit for sales it didn’t drive, according to internal communications and people with knowledge of the matter.”

item.title: Alaska lawmakers must think twice about blocking on Facebook
item.description: Center Square: “The Alaska Supreme Court won’t let state lawmakers block members of the public on Facebook and delete their comments, rejecting the appeal of a minor punishment imposed on a former state senator.”

item.title: German advocacy group lodges criminal complaint over Meta AI glasses
item.description: Reuters: “A German advocacy group has filed a criminal complaint ‌against Meta and other companies selling the technology group’s AI glasses in Germany, arguing the devices violate privacy laws.:

item.title: Scottish Council on Archives Launches Two New Toolkits
item.description: Scottish Council on Archives: “The Deposited Collections Online Toolkit provides practical guidance, model agreements, case studies, and advocacy materials to support archivists and archive holders in managing deposited and loaned collections…. The Accessible Records Management Online Toolkit offers plain-language guidance, templates, and case studies for people with records management responsibilities who are newly qualified or working without formal training — including staff in charities, small public bodies, community organisations, and private businesses.”

item.title: Closed Door Romance database
item.description: New-to-me: the A closed door romance is a romance where the sexual/intimate contact takes place “off-camera.” The site contains over 2000 books, filterable in a number of ways.

item.title: Czech Republic: A new database and map that document Holocaust monuments and memorials throughout the Czech Republic has been launched
item.description: Jewish Heritage Europe: “A new database and specialized map that systematically document Holocaust monuments and memorials located throughout the Czech Republic has been launched… It currently contains 616 detailed records and more than 5,550 photographs, representing a total of 10 GB of data.”

item.title: WordPress 7.0.4 Release
item.description: WordPress: “WordPress 7.0.4 is now available which features a security fix. Because this is a security release, it is recommended that you update your sites immediately.”

item.title: Stream free movies and shows on Google TV Freeplay
item.description: Google Blog: “You can now watch more than 10,000 free movies and shows whenever you want on Google TV Freeplay. We’re also expanding our TV lineup to include more than 300 free live channels.”

item.title: Photos, memes, and conspiracies out of the 2026 solar eclipse
item.description: Mashable: “For the first time in 27 years, the people of mainland Europe were able to watch the moon pass perfectly in front of the sun and blot out its earthbound rays. That means members of Gen Alpha, and many young Gen Z space enthusiasts, just experienced their very first total solar eclipse.”

item.title: Sports Photographer Has Instagram Account Wrongfully Banned by Meta Over ‘Sexualization of Children’
item.description: PetaPixel: “A sports photographer had his Instagram account permanently disabled after Meta mistakenly claimed his content violated its rules against the ‘sexualization of children.’ 19-year-old photographer and videographer Jack Rastorfer creates and edits high-energy videos featuring athletes and sporting events for social media.”

item.title: CISA Unveils New Cybersecurity Resources for K-12 Schools and Districts
item.description: CISA: “The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) today released the K-12 Cybersecurity Foundations Resource Package, a comprehensive collection of guides, videos and supplemental materials to help K‑12 schools and districts prevent, mitigate and respond to prevalent cyber threats.”

item.title: FBI warns hackers are breaking into social media accounts to steal and sell users’ nude photos
item.description: TechSpot: “The FBI has issued a warning for anyone who likes to take explicit photos (i.e., nudes) of themselves. Hackers are targeting both adult and underage users by compromising their social media and personal accounts to steal these images and sell them on criminal marketplaces – and they often include details about the victims.”

item.title: Making history accessible: Doug Boyd’s CURATE research
item.description: University of Kentucky: “‘Oral history is one of the greatest documents that can be created,’ said Doug Boyd, Ph.D., director of the University of Kentucky Libraries Louie B. Nunn Center for Oral History. ‘It puts individuals on the historical record, and that is really a remarkable thing.’ Boyd has been reimagining how those historical records are accessed. Traditional oral history often sat on library shelves for decades without being heard, but Boyd’s research focuses on the intersection of technology and community to ensure these voices are discoverable and used by the public.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: See the hideous AI version of Queen’s The Game that sparked Brian May rant
item.description: Gold Radio: “While a number of artists have embraced AI as a new tool in their creative arsenal, it seems that Brian May is not going to be convinced of its merits any time soon. The Queen guitarist has gone on a rant against the technology after asking one image generator to re-create the cover of The Game album, with hideous – and hilarious – consequences.”

item.title: Grok Gets Cursor-Driven Upgrade, Claims to Be Competitive With Top Models
item.description: Gizmodo: “Thus far in its short lifespan, the AI model Grok is probably best known for being used to mass-produce non-consensual nude images and for declaring itself MechaHitler. So it’s an uphill battle to convince people to use it for coding and knowledge work. But for those heavily invested in keeping tabs on the benchmarks of AI models, the release of Grok 4.6, which was made publicly available on Wednesday, might be compelling.”

item.title: Amazon will train on Twitch streamers’ content by default, unless they opt out
item.description: TechCrunch: “The streaming platform Twitch will now use creators’ content to help train generative AI models for its parent company, Amazon. This move has inspired swift and concentrated backlash from the Twitch community, especially because creators are opted in to having their content used for this AI training by default.”

item.title: State Board roundup, 8.12.26: AI standards approved for K-12 schools
item.description: Idaho Ed News: “The Idaho State Board of Education on Wednesday approved a set of standards that will guide how K-12 public schools deal with artificial intelligence. State lawmakers this year passed a law directing the Idaho Department of Education to develop an AI framework. IDE then convened a committee with dozens of educators and industry experts who wrote the framework.”

item.title: Schools spend billions on AI, but struggle to figure out what’s worth buying
item.description: Stateline: “As a new school year begins, some classrooms may use artificial intelligence tools to flag a student struggling with classwork, track attendance or try to raise reading scores. But as school districts make decisions on which tools are safe and worth spending thousands or millions of dollars on, some officials feel overwhelmed by the array of choices.”

item.title: Cornell expands AI Critical Literacy Program for incoming students
item.description: Cornell Chronicle: “After a successful pilot launch in the spring, Cornell’s AI Critical Literacy Program will be offered in the fall to all incoming students as well as other interested students, faculty members and staff. The expanded program will feature four modules – ‘What is Generative AI?’; ‘Ethical Questions Surrounding Generative AI’; ‘GenAI and Learning’; and ‘Creating an AI Policy for Personal Use’ – via the web-based learning platform Canvas.”

item.title: House lawmakers visit Vatican to discuss AI — and meet the pope
item.description: Politico: “A bipartisan House delegation met with top Vatican officials on Wednesday to discuss artificial intelligence during a visit that briefly included Pope Leo XIV, according to two people with knowledge of the trip granted anonymity to disclose details of the private meetings.”

item.title: Axios Wants to Save Local News with AI
item.description: Columbia Journalism Review: “Every media company faces existential questions about the rise of AI, especially this one: How should newsrooms get paid for the information AI spits out and the models that were trained on journalists’ work? The New York Times has sought to answer this question in court. Some (including the Times) have struck licensing deals. But as most newsrooms scramble to limit AI’s damage, [Jim] VandeHei has been among the loudest voices arguing it may well do some good.”

item.title: I Tested a Popular A.I. Slop Detector. It Felt Empowering.
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “I tested Pangram, which costs $20 a month, for about a week and tried all sorts of experiments to challenge the system. I fed it personal essays alongside text generated with chatbots instructed to imitate my writing. I also uploaded social media posts from LinkedIn and Reddit that I suspected were A.I.-generated. In dozens of tests, the detector never failed at distinguishing slop from human writing.”

item.title: Tech innovator uses AI to rebuild David Webb’s Hong Kong database
item.description: South China Morning Post: “Keith Li King-wah, co-founder and principal trainer of Allytic AI, announced on his Facebook page on Wednesday that he would rebuild [David] Webb-site’s database of 27 years with the use of artificial intelligence (AI).”

item.title: Taiwan says it was targeted last month in AI-driven hacking campaign
item.description: Reuters: “Taiwan has in recent years complained about what it sees as China’s ‘hybrid warfare’ — from daily military drills near the island to disinformation campaigns and cyberattacks — as Beijing ramps up military and political pressure on the democratically governed island to force Taipei to accept its claims of sovereignty.”

item.title: ‘Near-autonomous’ AI agents attack Taiwan’s nuclear safety agency
item.description: The Register: “Suspected Chinese cyber operatives used publicly available AI tools to compromise Taiwanese government systems before expanding the attack to its nuclear safety agency, supply-chain vendors, and at least seven energy companies in what security researchers called a ‘near-autonomous attack.'”

item.title: Grading Tomatoes With An ESP32 And ML
item.description: Hackaday: “If you’ve ever worked with produce, you might know about grading. In addition to deciding if, say, a strawberry is good or not, they also have to sort them by color. Turns out, you don’t care if one package of berries is a bit redder than another, but you do care if one package has too much color variation. [Pmalfa31] applied an ESP32 and machine learning to grading tomatoes.”

item.title: Peer review is overwhelmed—can it survive in the AI era?
item.description: Ars Technica: “The number of papers indexed in the databases Scopus and Web of Science, for example, has recently been increasing exponentially, at a rate of 5.6 percent per year. By one estimate, researchers around the globe are devoting a collective 15,000 years of work to peer review every year—work that, if paid, would cost $1.5 billion for the share done in the US alone. Increasingly, researchers are finding it hard to donate that kind of time.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: New Database Documents Over 100 Cases of Cops Abusing Flock Surveillance Cameras
item.description: Common Dreams: “A new database launched Wednesday that details more than 100 cases of alleged abuse by law enforcement officers using Flock Safety’s nationwide camera network is adding fresh urgency to the growing backlash against automated license plate readers.”

item.title: Apple Removes Yandex’s Payment Service App
item.description: Moscow Times: “Major Russian digital wallet and payment service Yandex Pay said Wednesday that its application had been removed from Apple’s App Store. The removal means iPhone users in Russia can no longer download or update Yandex Pay. The app allows users to store cards, make contactless payments and split purchases across Yandex’s suite of services.”

item.title: Google Renews Battle With SerpApi Over Scraping
item.description: MediaPost: “Renewing its battle with SerpApi, Google this week filed an amended complaint alleging that the Texas-based company — which provides data to other businesses — bypassed attempts to prevent it from scraping search results.”

item.title: This site lets you compare frontier AI models with your own prompt (and for free
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Sure, newer models are better, but people have preferences, and certain models may provide better results than others. I, for example, prefer to use Claude Sonnet 5 because it’s usually straightforward and uses fewer fluff words. The problem is that trying different AI models usually means jumping between different websites, creating accounts, and dealing with separate usage limits. Arena.ai changes that by bringing them together in a single interface.” Please note the caveat about privacy at the end of the article.

item.title: Belgian Gamer Michiel Vandeweert Dies at 28, Doubling Progeria Life Expectancy
item.description: Shane the Gamer: “Belgian content creator and gamer Michiel Vandeweert has died at 28, more than twice as long as doctors expected when he was diagnosed as a child with progeria, the ultra-rare genetic disorder that causes rapid aging.”

item.title: Google opens first directly run store outside U.S. in Tokyo
item.description: Japan Times: “U.S. technology giant Google opened its first directly run store outside the United States in Tokyo’s fashionable Omotesando district Thursday. The store sells smartphones and offers repair services.”

item.title: Lawsuit seeks to ban Trump Media from charging for early access to president’s posts on US policy
item.description: Associated Press: “The lawsuit alleges the service offering paying customers sneak peeks of his posts about U.S. policy on war, tariffs and other issues violates the Constitution and that official announcements should be made available to everyone at the same time. The new subscription service rolled out earlier this month is charging Wall Street firms as much as $100,000 a month to trade off the market-moving posts before others.”

item.title: Judge lets SEO sabotage lawsuit over toxic backlinks move forward
item.description: Search Engine Land: “A federal judge refused to dismiss a lawsuit alleging an auto transport company used toxic backlinks to hurt a competitor’s Google rankings.”

item.title: Digitizing super 8 film yourself
item.description: Nibble Stew: “In our previous post we looked at fixing a super 8 film projector. While watching film with a real projector has its own charm, it is inconvenient to say the least. … Even if you manage not to burn the film, merely running it through the projector causes wear, scratches and tearing. While film typically ages very well, eventually it will turn into magenta goop or gets eaten by vinegar syndrome. Thus you really want to convert all these films into high quality digital files.”

item.title: Study links short-form video addiction to a decline in teenagers’ academic coping skills
item.description: PsyPost: “A recent study of high school students reveals that addictive use of short-form video apps predicts a decline in a student’s ability to handle everyday academic stress.”

item.title: Digitizing Hidden Collections: Amplifying Unheard Voices Application Now Open
item.description: Council on Library and Information Resources: “The Council on Library and Information Resources (CLIR) is now accepting applications for the fifth cycle of Digitizing Hidden Collections: Amplifying Unheard Voices (DHC:AUV), generously underwritten by the Mellon Foundation. The program awards grants ranging from $50,000 to $300,000 to digitize rare and unique materials that deepen the public understanding of underrepresented communities, including people of the global majority, disabled populations, Indigenous voices, LGBTQ+ communities, immigrants, displaced persons, the incarcerated, and others that have been insufficiently recognized or unattended.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Atari ST Public Floppy Database now open for everyone — online archive originally designed for ST flash cart packed with classics and homebrew
item.description: Tom’s Hardware: “An extensive Atari ST floppy disk database can now easily be accessed by all netizens. Originally created to serve floppy images to the owners of the SidecarTridge multi‑function hardware add‑on for the Atari ST family (ST, STE, Mega ST, TT, Falcon), anyone can now browse, search, and download the .ST files to use with other hardware, emulators, or even to rewrite the disk images to actual floppies.”

item.title: Google tests sponsored results with new subheading
item.description: Search Engine Watch: “Google is now testing a change that displays the websites name directly under sponsored results. Normally, sponsored results just carry the ‘Sponsored Results’ heading, but this test adds a subheading ‘from website icon and website name.'”

item.title: Bluesky’s active user base is shrinking as its focus expands beyond the app
item.description: TechCrunch: “According to data from digital intelligence provider Similarweb, Bluesky’s mobile app had 10.4 million monthly active users worldwide in June 2026, down 27.2% year-over-year. In addition, mobile daily active users continued to decline, falling 25.6% year-over-year in July to around 3 million.”

item.title: Neocities is Improving – And I Noticed!
item.description: Aywren: “As a daily user of the Neocities hosting platform, I’ve observed some quiet updates the site has begun to roll out over this past year. These things are sometimes hard to spot unless you use the site as much as I do, and there are no release notes out there that I can find.”

item.title: YouTube sensation Ms. Rachel announces debut album with Mr. Aron, ‘I’m So Happy’
item.description: Associated Press: “Parents of toddlers everywhere, prepare yourselves. YouTube sensation and music teacher Ms. Rachel and her husband, Aron Accurso, will release their debut album, the 23-track ‘I’m So Happy,’ on Sept. 25…. Ms. Rachel launched her mega popular YouTube channel in 2019 with her husband, known online as Mr. Aron.”

item.title: Streetwise Opera awarded £189K grant to collate 25th anniversary archive
item.description: The Stage: “Through recordings, photographs, scores, programmes and designs, Streetwise Opera will document its history of work with people who have experienced homelessness to co-create new opera from diverse voices.”

item.title: A cybersecurity researcher covered a Toyota in an AI-generated pattern to confuse Flock cameras
item.description: TechSpot: “The pattern does not stop a camera from recording. Instead, it is designed to prevent the software connected to the camera from recognizing what it sees. A person or car wearing the pattern would still appear in the footage, but the detection system may not flag it as a person or vehicle.”

item.title: YouTube Premium kills the ads but doesn’t solve the real problem. Here’s the stack I use to do that.
item.description: Amerpie: “Paid for YouTube Premium after years of DIY ad-blocking. Ads are gone; the algorithm, the clutter, and the impermanence aren’t. Building a stack of small tools instead of hunting for one app that fixes all four. First post in a series; toolbox preview inside, full reviews coming.”

item.title: Bandcamp Archiver
item.description: Inkdroid: “There are already fine tools for downloading a Bandcamp collection: bandsnatch and the bandcamp-collection-downloader both fetch the lot, in parallel, in the format you want. But they know only what they downloaded, and what I needed to know was what I was missing. So I worked with Claude Code on bandcamp-archiver, which reads the embedded tags off my disk, compares that inventory against my Bandcamp purchases, and downloads the difference one album at a time.”

item.title: Tagging whales from the sky: New methods revolutionize research
item.description: University of Hawaii: “Marine mammal research has attained new heights as scientists at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa are deploying noninvasive suction-cup tags onto humpback whales using drones. Traditionally, researchers from the Marine Mammal Research Program (MMRP) in the Hawaiʻi Institute of Marine Biology approached animals closely via boats, deploying tags using a seven-meter carbon fiber pole. Now, technological advances are allowing the team to tag whales from the sky, dramatically shifting how marine data is collected.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Following the Fire Enhanced Data Strengthens Digital Conservation Decision-Making
item.description: USDA Natural Resources Conservation Service: “The SE FireMap Viewer 2.0 is a geospatial platform tool that helps land managers, fire practitioners, and conservation partners better understand where wildfires and prescribed fires are happening across the Southeast. The latest version significantly expands on its predecessor’s capabilities by offering improved, high-resolution tracking of historic fire patterns extending back 30 years, including fire frequency, fire free intervals, and the year of the last burn detection.”

item.title: MES opens interactive dashboard “Specialized publications of Ukraine”
item.description: The State Scientific And Technical Library Of Ukraine, and machine-translated from Ukrainian: “As part of the work of the Ministry of Education and Science of Ukraine to develop an open and transparent system of scientific professional publications, an interactive dashboard ‘Professional Publications of Ukraine’ was created. The State Service for Scientific and Technical Publications of Ukraine provided the digital infrastructure and administration of relevant data in the URIS system.”

item.title: Google is testing a new homepage that buries the search button for AI
item.description: TechSpot: “As spotted by Search Engine Watch, Google’s latest ‘experiment’ is a new Search homepage shown to users who have not signed into their Google Account. The new page encourages netizens to use more Google AI services, pushing traditional web search queries into the background.” Gross.

item.title: I tried Opera’s new vertical tabs – and it might be the best implementation yet
item.description: ZDNet: “I’ve been using Opera, on and off, for over a decade. The browser has several features that have become absolute musts for me, such as Workspaces, split screen, and a brilliant theming engine. But the one feature that has been missing all this time is vertical tabs.”

item.title: CLIR Awards Nearly $1 Million in Recordings at Risk Grant Funds
item.description: Council on Library and Information Resources: “The Council on Library and Information Resources (CLIR) is pleased to announce the thirteenth cohort of projects for Recordings at Risk, CLIR’s program that funds the digitization of rare and unique audio and audiovisual materials. An independent review panel selected 24 projects for funding from an applicant pool of 94, totaling $993,170 in grant funds. Work on these year-long projects will begin September 1, 2026.”

item.title: The Creators of VHS Dates Are Ready to Come Clean
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “Viewers, including some celebrities, were touched by the onscreen vulnerability, as well as the outfits and hairstyles that looked like something out of an old Sears catalog. I, too, found it compelling. I scheduled an interview with the two filmmakers who said they had been digitizing the footage. Their publicist explicitly told me these were ‘real’ dating tapes. But when I showed up to meet them at a cavernous studio near downtown Los Angeles, they said, ‘This is where we shoot the videos.'”

item.title: Microsoft Plugs Nearly 400 Security Holes
item.description: Krebs on Security: “Microsoft today released updates to remedy at least 398 security vulnerabilities in its Windows operating systems and supported software, including one weakness that is already being actively exploited and two others that were publicly detailed prior to today.”

item.title: Signal adds an extra layer of security to make sure you’re actually chatting with the right person
item.description: The Register: “Signal has introduced a new layer of security to help make sure no one has secretly interfered with your encrypted chats. The chat app is favored by diplomats, activists, and journalists for its security. It uses end-to-end message encryption and ‘safety numbers’ – cryptographic fingerprints associated with the keys securing a conversation – which users can compare to verify they have the expected encrypted connection with a contact.”

item.title: We analyzed 6,400 New York Times stories to find out how comments change when you give readers more information
item.description: NiemanLab: “Data journalists have sometimes wondered whether loading a story with data can be overwhelming rather than clarifying. We found that giving readers more information changes who comments, and how.”

item.title: Disinformation that spreads during heat waves
item.description: Science Literacy Project: “Extreme weather typically brings a storm of disinformation with it; this [summer 2026] heat wave is no different.”

item.title: A Palestinian Village Destroyed in 1953 Is Being Rebuilt in VR
item.description: WIRED Middle East: “Using oral histories, archival photographs and British maps, Palestinian diaspora architect Tony Ghannam is reconstructing Kafr Bir’im as it existed before its residents were displaced in 1948.”

item.title: “Binge Thinking” aims to provide an antidote to doomscrolling
item.description: Cambridge Day: “[Sara] Wasserman, an associate professor of neuroscience at Wellesley College, was the featured speaker for the pop-lecture series, ‘Binge Thinking.’ The lecture series, which invites local professors to give talks at Boston and Cambridge area bars, is the brainchild of founder Rory Madigan, who works at a think tank in Cambridge.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Farmer trusted AI after it gave good advice, then it helped wipe out 25 acres of his crops
item.description: TechSpot: “Most readers of this site know not to blindly trust AI on important matters, even if it got things right before. A farmer in Chuzhou, China, discovered this the hard way when he took weed and pest control advice from a chatbot. The result was the death of 25 acres of crops.”

item.title: As datacenters expand, so does public opposition to them
item.description: The Register: “Anti-datacenter sentiment appears to be hardening in the US and UK, with more American jurisdictions blocking new builds and protesters marching against a planned facility in London’s historic Brick Lane. A burst of new projects on both sides of the Atlantic has brought concerns about electricity bills, water supplies, and massive warehouse-like structures looming over nearby homes.”

item.title: Georgia data centers likely to demand more energy than the state can provide
item.description: The Current Georgia: “Last year, Georgia Power got permission from the state’s Public Service Commission to radically increase the amount of electricity the utility generates and sells. The reason data centers. Now as communities across the state make deals with data center developers, there’s reason to believe Georgia has promised more power than it has to offer — even after Georgia Power’s expansion.”

item.title: Mississippi should set rules before data centers continue growing, Sen. Hillman Frazier says
item.description: Mississippi Today: “Mississippi has an opportunity before it. Across the country, states are competing to attract data centers and the investment they promise. New jobs, new tax revenue and new technology are all things worth pursuing. But as a state senator, I believe we have another responsibility that is just as important: making sure the people who live here aren’t left asking questions after decisions have already been made.”

item.title: Here’s how to find information about data centers in Texas
item.description: Texas Tribune: “What information is accessible about a data center project can differ from place to place and depend on whether a project seeks out tax breaks, whether it needs local rezoning or special permits, and how it will get its power and water. Here are some ways Texans and policy experts are tracking down information about data centers through local and state public records or private data companies.”

item.title: 8 local AI models that run great on 8GB of VRAM or less
item.description: MakeUseOf: “Running a local AI model usually requires painfully high VRAM, and not everyone has the latest monster GPU with the coveted yet still absurd 20-plus gigabytes of VRAM. Thankfully, there do exist a few surprisingly capable, lightweight alternatives that (depending on your exact use case) might even surprise you with what they can do, whether you’re on AMD or Nvidia.”

item.title: You Can (Maybe) Run Meta’s Latest AI Model Locally on Your Computer
item.description: Lifehacker: “On Monday, Meta announced its latest AI model: Muse Glimmer. The company isn’t necessarily advertising this model as its biggest and best, however. While Meta has plenty to say about Muse Glimmer’s performance potential, there are two key selling points for the model in the company’s eyes: The fact that it’s open-weight, and that it’s designed to run locally on ‘consumer’ Macs and PCs—though perhaps not on your computer.”

item.title: Rep. Julia Letlow bought Meta stock after signing an NDA with the company, records show
item.description: Louisiana Illuminator: “U.S. Rep. Julia Letlow signed a nondisclosure agreement with Laidley LLC — a shell company of Meta Platforms — on June 29, 2024, giving her access to confidential details about the tech giant’s plans for a $50 billion data center in Richland Parish, according to the document obtained by the Gulf States Newsroom. Within months, she began buying stock in Meta and Nvidia, the company whose chips power Meta’s data centers.”

item.title: Authors face backlash for participation in 2022 Google AI study
item.description: Engadget: “In the spring of 2022, Google began reaching out to a series of writers, including award-winning science-fiction authors and New York Times bestsellers, for feedback on an experimental writing tool. Four years later, their participation has corners of the literary world up in arms.”

item.title: Google confirms testing new buttons on home page to drive users to AI-powered search features
item.description: Search Engine Land: “Google is testing new buttons on the Google home page, right beneath the search box, to encourage searchers to try out AI Mode and other AI-powered search features. The buttons are named create images, ask about files and brainstorm and when clicked on, it takes you into AI Mode.” No thanks, I’m good.

item.title: Disney Plus tries a new AI-powered search
item.description: The Verge: “Disney is testing a new AI-powered tool for Disney Plus that uses a natural language search, a voice query, or a suggested prompt to create a customized row of show and movie recommendations.”

item.title: North Korean spies are running local LLMs to cause AI mischief
item.description: The Register: “The researchers said they observed Kimsuky setting up and operating local LLM environments using Ollama, GPT4All, and Msty, experimenting with other AI tools such as Cursor, and using retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for local document searches. This prevents the data from getting sucked into the cloud where enemies might see it and try to stop it.”

item.title: China bets on AI weather forecasting as extreme weather intensifies
item.description: Reuters: “For decades, weather prediction has relied on numerical models running ​on supercomputers that simulate atmospheric physics. AI models instead learn patterns from vast archives of ⁠historical weather observations and can produce forecasts in a fraction of the time. The technology is increasingly being tested during ​typhoon season in East Asia, where even small improvements in track forecasts can help authorities better prepare for flooding, organise evacuations and manage ​potential transport disruptions.”

item.title: Senior nursing students study community health impacts of Boyce data center project
item.description: Northwestern State University of Louisiana: “Senior Bachelor of Science in Nursing students at Northwestern State University’s Cenla campus studied community health concerns surrounding a data center under construction in Boyce through a Level 5 community impact project.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Richard Samuel Roberts Collection digitized
item.description: Columbia Star: “Richard Samuel Roberts became one of South Carolina’s most famous photographers in the 1920s and 1930s. However, after his death in 1936, Roberts remained relatively unknown to all but his family and those who had been his closest friends for more than four decades. His work was brought back to the public with a display at the Columbia Museum and a book in 1986. Now his entire collection has been published online through the University of South Carolina’s Library System.”

item.title: Malaysia Was Confident in Its Social Media Ban, but Kids Are Still Logged In
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “The authorities have asked social media companies to explain their failure to comply with the ban and detail the measures they have taken to implement age verification mechanisms, the Ministry of Communications said in a statement last week. They now have until January 2027 to comply with the ban, according to Kamaruddin Abdul Rani, the under secretary of the control and compliance division of the ministry.”

item.title: Trump’s media company, which also owns Truth Social, reports $238m loss
item.description: The Guardian: “Donald Trump’s media company – which owns the Truth Social platform favored by the US president – posted a $238m loss in the second quarter.”

item.title: Film photography blogs you should follow
item.description: Down the Road: “It’s time for my annual roundup of film-photography blogs. Some blogs last for a short time while others last for decades. But the film-photography blogging community remains strong. There are 121 active blogs here! Since last year, 14 blogs either closed or stopped posting. But 23 blogs are either new or have returned after a pause.”

item.title: Historian Jill Lepore says Silicon Valley misreads science fiction and undermines democracy
item.description: TechCrunch: “In her upcoming book ‘The Rise and Fall of the Artificial State,’ Jill Lepore warns that tech companies are increasingly replacing the functions of democratic government. This shift, she said, marks ‘a return to tyranny and mystification in the form of rule by algorithms, corporations, machines.'”

item.title: Meta and TikTok agree to fact-check content on Spain border crossings after deadly rush
item.description: Reuters: “Social networks Meta and TikTok have agreed to fact-check content ​on border crossings into Spain following the massive rush ‌to enter the Spanish enclave of Ceuta from Morocco, European Union tech chief Henna Virkkunen said.”

item.title: FBI teams with the NCAA to help athletes avoid sexual exploitation
item.description: Associated Press: “The FBI is teaming with the NCAA to start a program to combat sexual exploitation of college athletes whose private images are increasingly found and targeted online in an era when they use their name, image and likeness to enhance their own marketability.”

item.title: Ohio looks to file class-action lawsuit against Roblox
item.description: Spectrum News 1: “Ohio Attorney General Andy Wilson is seeking a lead class-action lawsuit against video game developer Roblox. He filed a motion to lead the case on behalf of the Ohio Public Employees Retirement System and the State Teachers Retirement System of Ohio.”

item.title: Granite Geek: Science Cafe returns to Concord as the internet falls apart
item.description: Concord Monitor: “This carnage on click-throughs caused by A.I. summaries is so great and happening so quickly that NPR has called it an ‘extinction-level event’ for journalism sites dependent on viewership-based ad revenue. The industry is brainstorming how to react, but a decade of watching us in the media whipsawed by internet technologies makes me doubt there is a solution. Unless the government breaks up Google — yeah, like that’s going to happen — I think the Internet Era for Traditional Media is over.”

item.title: How disinformation on X imperils Japan’s democracy
item.description: Japan Times: “Tokyo cannot simply stand by while a foreign-owned private platform serves as a pipeline for national destabilization. The Japanese government must take concrete, structural steps to build digital resilience and provide trusted alternatives. First, Japan must support the establishment of an independent, nonpartisan Public Information Verification Network.” Good afternoon, Internet…

item.title: Former federal data officials answer the question: How many federal datasets have been terminated since January 2025?
item.description: PR Newswire: (PRESS RELEASE). “Today, dataindex.us, the nation’s leading resource for monitoring changes to federal data, published the Federal Data Terminations Tracker—the most policy-relevant, verified source of federal datasets terminated since January 2025. Having evolved from the crowdsourced Dearly Departed Datasets published in October 2025, the tracker combines community reporting with expert identification and review to provide a regularly updated record of terminations.”

item.title: Thousands of Indian WW1 soldiers to be remembered in perpetuity after historical injustice
item.description: BFBS Forces News: “The British Army’s Major Daljinder Singh Virdee, a driving force behind Sikh recognition in defence, expressed how he felt to BFBS Forces News after the Commonwealth War Graves Commission (CWGC) announced the largest single addition to its casualty records since the Second World War that will help create a more inclusive narrative of the First World War.”

item.title: https://citeme.app
item.description: Daniel N. let me know about his new site, the revamped CiteMe ( ) CiteMe rang a bell so I asked him when it launched. He replied “The site originally launched in 2024 as a citation generator, built around a Chrome extension. I bought it in January 2026 and rebuilt it completely. The old version generated citations with a language model, which is exactly how fabricated references get made. The current version doesn’t generate them, it looks them up in real scholarly records (OpenAlex, Crossref, PubMed, Europe PMC, arXiv) and returns what it actually finds. The reference checker the part that takes a bibliography and flags references it can’t verify against those records, launched in March 2026.”

item.title: SpaceX’s Earnings Show Elon Wiped Out Two-Thirds Of Twitter’s Ad Business
item.description: Techdirt: “In the 10-Q, all of X’s revenue is now (misleadingly) labeled “AI” revenue, but even then the reporting has to admit ad revenue took a big hit, dropping $160 million compared to the first half of 2025 (which was already way, way, way lower than when Elon took over the site), going from $870 million in 2025 to $710 million in the first half of 2026.”

item.title: YouTube now requires creators to have twice as many watch hours to start earning money
item.description: TechCrunch: “Creators who want to start earning on the platform will need at least 8,000 qualified watch hours over the past year or 20 million qualified Shorts views in the last 90 days. Currently, creators need 1,000 subscribers and 4,000 watch hours over the past year or 1,000 subscribers and 10 million Shorts views over the past 90 days.”

item.title: Students can get these 4 expensive apps for free
item.description: How-To Geek: “Many students can get access to professional software suites for free simply because they’re enrolled in school. Depending on what you’re studying, that can include productivity apps, design tools, programming software, and other programs that would normally cost hundreds of dollars. Before you start paying for software this semester, these are four free options worth checking first.”

item.title: Meta/Facebook Crawling Web & May Be Building Search Engine
item.description: Search Engine Roundtable: “Meta, the social media company that operates Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, Messenger, and Threads, is allegedly crawling the web and in the process of building its own search engine.”

item.title: French press body asks competition watchdog to take action over Google AI
item.description: Reuters: “A French press association has asked ​the country’s competition watchdog to take action against ‌Google’s artificial intelligence-generated article summaries, which the trade group says deprive newspapers and magazines of readers.”

item.title: US prosecutors want Tate brothers to remain in custody as they fight extradition to the UK
item.description: Associated Press: “Prosecutors want social media influencers Andrew and Tristan Tate to remain in federal custody, arguing Monday that the brothers are a flight risk and a danger to the community, as they fight extradition to the United Kingdom, where the brothers are accused of rape and sex trafficking.”

item.title: National Gallery Accused of ‘Soft Censorship’ to Avoid Provoking Trump
item.description: New York Times: This link goes to a gift article. “[Steven] Nelson acknowledged that the gallery leaders’ intentions in moving the symposium, which had been inspired by its exhibition on the Black artist Elizabeth Catlett, were in some respects an effort to save it. But he worried that the institution had restricted free speech by limiting access to the event at a time when the Trump administration was looking to reframe American history.”

item.title: Google Search Is Dying. What Comes Next Is Worse
item.description: The Walrus: “The corpus is collapsing in real time. This degraded digital space should force a broader understanding of cultural sovereignty. Right now, the debate is framed largely as a fight over whether foreign mega platforms like Netflix, YouTube, or Spotify should support Canadian content. That charged conversation sidesteps the deeper question: Who preserves and controls access to our cultural record—not just in the present but for generations after?”

item.title: How data journalism is done on TikTok: six key takeaways from watching 50 videos
item.description: Online Journalism Blog: “In a guest post for OJB, James Hickman pulls together a set of basic best-practice guidelines for creating data journalism videos on TikTok, from length and location to animation and style.” Good morning, Internet…

item.title: Ancient Newa manuscripts maintained online with Japanese support
item.description: Radio Nepal Online: ” In partnership with UNESCO, Archive Nepal has digitized more than 30 rare and endangered manuscripts dating back 200 to 800 years with the support of the Japanese government.”

item.title: Ogeechee Riverkeeper announces Burroughs Digital Library of Ogeechee River images
item.description: Grice Connect: “In 2025, Ogeechee Riverkeeper (ORK) received a grant from the Karen and Jerry Burroughs Foundation Fund of The Savannah Community Foundation, to research, create, and curate aerial imagery of the Ogeechee River basin.”

item.title: Made by Google 2026 Launch Live: Pixel 11, Pixel 11 Pro Fold, Pixel Watch 5, Gemini, and all the news
item.description: Android Central: “We hope you’re as excited to learn about Google’s latest smartphones as we are! Last year’s launch was filled with celebrities and internet personalities, and this year looks to be no different, with Stephen Curry, Shubman Gill, Ayami Nakajo, and more, with Trevor Noah hosting. Over the next few days, we’ll be going over what you can expect and covering the event live as it happens so you don’t have to miss a thing!” The event is not until the 12th but the site is already update with pre-event news/information.

item.title: Following Epic loss, Google has started hosting rival app stores in the Play Store
item.description: Ars Technica: “A new day has dawned in the Play Store, and it’s one that Google tried very hard to avoid. The first third-party app store has arrived in Google Play as a result of the long-running antitrust lawsuit with Epic. Those in the US can now head into Google Play and download Aptoide, a game-focused store that has been available as a sideloaded client since the early days of Android.”

item.title: RAF Museum Launches Red Arrows Challenge to Support Preservation and Education
item.description: Vintage Aviation News: “The RAF Museum has launched the Red Arrows Challenge, a nationwide fundraising event running from Aug. 1 to Oct. 3. Participants can walk, run, or cycle at their own pace while supporting the museum’s preservation and education work, with commemorative rewards, fundraising prizes, and a chance to meet the Royal Air Force’s iconic Red Arrows display team.”

item.title: Wayne State Acquires Casey Kasem and American Top 40 Collection from Radio Historian Pete Battistini
item.description: Wayne State University: “Pete Battistini has been chasing Casey Kasem’s American Top 40 (AT40) for more than 50 years. In 1971, Battistini heard AT40 for the first time and was instantly captivated, and the passion that followed turned into one of the largest collections of AT40 in the world– and part of that collection now has a permanent home at the Walter P. Reuther Library.”

item.title: US court rules Meta, other tech companies must face thousands of lawsuits over social media addiction
item.description: Reuters: “The San Francisco-based 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected the companies’ bid to reverse a lower court’s ruling forcing them to face more than 3,000 lawsuits over the claims filed in federal court, concluding that the appeal came too early in ​the litigation.”

item.title: Does Google Search favor a liberal view on immigration?
item.description: PsyPost: “Google search results for immigration topics tend to present an overall positive view of the issue, according to a recent analysis of Swedish search data. The research, published in Heliyon, found that while the links skew slightly positive, the search engine tends to place neutral, unpoliticized sources at the very top of the page.”

item.title: Old Tibetan Prints, New Digital Access: PechaBridge and the Digital Collections at Stabi
item.description: CrossAsia: “Digitization makes historical Tibetan pecha prints visible online, but visibility alone does not make their content readable, searchable, or reusable for research. PechaBridge is an open-source pipeline connecting digitized materials from the Staatsbibliothek zu Berlin with layout analysis, Tibetan OCR, metadata, and review tools.”

item.title: Chicago’s first-ever ‘cat tour’ brings a day of whimsy to Lincoln Square: ‘I think people need it’
item.description: Chicago Sun-Times: “For two hours, attendees hopped from house to house to view more than 125 residents’ cats on porches, or in windows and yards. … One participant rolled her own cat in a stroller. Some used the official Google Map to go rogue, while others joined one of four guided routes with relevant names: Chonk, Zoomies, Primordial Pouch and Toe Beans.” Good afternoon, Internet…
